2048 Tile Ramp

Every tile colour, measured. L* under each number is its lightness; the chip between two tiles is ΔE2000, how different they look to a person. 1.0 is the smallest difference anyone can detect, and under 5 reads as the same colour mid-game.

Board

Live now

Starts on blue. The 4-through-32 run is the flattest stretch left, bottoming out at ΔE 10.49.

Proposed

Opens on orchid, no jump at 2→4, and the blues carry a steady lightness climb instead of hue alone.

What the spacing is doing now. The stops are no longer sampled at even intervals of a curve — that is what produced the ΔE 36.7 jump at 2→4 and the flat blues. A dense path is drawn through LCh, then eleven stops are placed on it by binary search for the largest distance at which all eleven still fit, and nudged afterwards to even out what slack remains.

The blues needed lightness, not hue. Cyan is perceptually compressed: rotating hue through it buys far less separation than the same rotation through greens or golds. The old lightness curve flattened as it approached its peak, parking four tiles inside three points of lightness right in that stretch, so they had nothing left to separate them. Lightness now runs in two straight segments and never flattens, which is what lifts 4→8 and 8→16 to ΔE 16.7 and 15.2.

Two honest limits. 16→32 and 32→64 sit at ΔE 11.4 — the cyan compression is a real ceiling, not something more search will fix. And 1024→2048 is ΔE 32: the terminal red is pinned and sits well below the rest of the ramp in lightness, so the last step is always going to be a long one. Both are at points where you rarely hold the two tiles side by side, which is why I left them.

Nothing is near-white. The solver reaches for pale colours every time it is allowed to, because they buy separation cheaply — an earlier pass put 32 at L* 94, practically white. Tiles are now capped at L* 88, so the palest is 85.4. That costs a little separation and keeps every tile a colour rather than a highlight, on both grounds.

Measured in CIE Lab from the display-p3 values, which is what the Pixel actually shows. Solver: tools/make_gradient.py.
